hook.support: Think of a local group that does good things. A footy club. A food bank. An animal shelter. They need people to help. Can you make something that gets people on board?
hook.core: Your local animal shelter needs volunteers. The junior footy club needs coaches. The community garden needs hands. They’re doing good work, but nobody knows. Your job: make something that gets people to care, and then to act.
hook.extend: Community groups live or die by whether people hear about them. Advocacy texts, such as brochures, webpages and posts, exist to get an audience to care and act. Making one that works takes research, design and drafting, then honest feedback and revision.

why.support: Groups need help. A good brochure or post can bring people in.
why.core: Every club, charity and community group needs people who can promote it. It’s a skill you can use for any cause you care about.
why.extend: Advocacy is how causes win support. Designing, drafting and revising promotional material for a real group is the core skill of community and marketing work.

articles.title: Get people on board

body.support:
To **advocate** means to speak up for someone or something. You can advocate for a group that helps people.

Groups need **volunteers**, money and members. A **brochure**, a webpage or a post can help.

**Answer four questions:**
- What is the problem?
- What does the group do?
- How can people help?
- How do they get in touch?
.
**Make it work:**
- Use a strong headline.
- Show real people in photos.
- Tell one short story.
- Give one clear thing to do. “Come on Saturday.”.
- Add contact details.
.
**Then fix it.**
- Write a **draft** first.
- Ask someone for **feedback**.
- **Revise** it. Make it better.
- Check your spelling.
body.core:
To **advocate** is to speak up for a person, group or idea. Community groups, like sports clubs, food banks, shelters and youth groups, need people to advocate for them. They need **volunteers**, members and donations.

**What goes in an advocacy text?** Whether it’s a **brochure**, a webpage or a post, readers need answers to four questions:
- **The problem:** why does this group matter?
- **The solution:** what does the group do about it?
- **The ask:** what can the reader do? (volunteer, donate, join, share).
- **The details:** when, where, how to get in touch.

**Features that work:**
- a headline that grabs attention and speaks to the reader.
- photos of real people doing real things.
- one short story or quote from someone the group has helped.
- a single, clear call to action.
- logo, contact details and socials.

**Draft, edit and revise.** Good promotional material is rewritten several times.
- **Draft:** get your ideas down.
- **Feedback:** show it to someone from your audience. Ask: what’s the message? Would you act?
- **Revise:** change the big things. Is the headline strong? Is the ask clear?
- **Edit:** fix spelling, punctuation and layout last.
body.extend:
To **advocate** is to speak up in public for a person, group or cause. Community groups rely on it to find **volunteers**, members and donors.

**Structure.** Strong advocacy texts often follow a problem, solution, action pattern. That is true of a **brochure**, a webpage or a post:
- **problem:** the need, made real and local.
- **solution:** what the group does, and proof that it helps.
- **action:** one specific thing the reader can do.
- **details:** when, where and how to get in touch.

**Features.**
- a headline addressed to the reader.
- real photos of real people.
- a **testimonial** or short story that builds a connection.
- facts from the group itself.
- branding: logo, colours and a steady tone.

**The values behind it.** Advocacy texts appeal to values like community, fairness and belonging. Match the values to your audience.

**Process.** Promotional writing takes several rounds:
- **draft** quickly.
- get **feedback** from your target audience, not just friends.
- **revise** the big things first: message, structure, call to action.
- **edit** spelling and punctuation last.

Evaluate it honestly: would *you* act on it?

caseStudies.title: One man, one harbour, 40,000 helpers

body.support:
**Ian Kiernan** was a builder and sailor from Sydney. He sailed alone around the world in a race.

On the way, he saw rubbish everywhere in the sea. He was shocked.

Back home, he asked people to help clean up **Sydney Harbour**. It happened on **8 January 1989**.

About **40,000** people came to help.

The next year, it became **Clean Up Australia Day**. Hundreds of thousands of people joined in, all over the country.

It started with one person who spoke up for a cause.
body.core:
**Ian Kiernan** was a Sydney builder and yachtsman. In the 1980s, he sailed solo around the world in a race. He was shocked by how much rubbish he saw floating in the oceans.

Back home, he and a group of friends organised **Clean Up Sydney Harbour** on **8 January 1989**. They expected a small turnout.

About **40,000** volunteers came.

The next year, the idea went national as **Clean Up Australia Day**. Hundreds of thousands of people took part across the country. Later, it went global as **Clean Up the World**.

The ask was simple and specific: turn up on one day, at one place, and pick up rubbish. That made it easy for people to say yes.
body.extend:
**Ian Kiernan** was a Sydney builder and yachtsman. During a solo round-the-world yacht race in the 1980s, he was struck by the amount of rubbish in the world’s oceans.

Back in Sydney, he and a committee of friends organised **Clean Up Sydney Harbour** on **8 January 1989**. About **40,000** volunteers turned up.

The following year it became **Clean Up Australia Day**, with hundreds of thousands of participants nationally. It later became **Clean Up the World**. Kiernan died in 2018.

The campaign’s advocacy worked for several reasons. The problem was visible and local: everyone could see the rubbish. The call to action was specific, achievable and time-bound: one day, one place, one task. Taking part was public and social, so it built a sense of community.

Advocacy doesn’t always need a big budget. It needs a clear problem, a clear ask, and a reason for people to say yes.

teacher.overview: Students learn the problem–solution–action structure and features of advocacy texts (headline, real images, testimonial, call to action, details), then create a brochure, webpage or post for a real community group. They draft, get audience feedback, revise big-picture elements, then edit conventions. The case study is Ian Kiernan’s Clean Up Sydney Harbour (1989), which drew about 40,000 volunteers with a simple, specific ask and grew into Clean Up Australia Day.
prep: Collect brochures and posts from local groups (council, library, sports clubs).
Consider partnering with a real local group; students’ work could be useful to them.
Arrange feedback partners (another class, family members, a local group).

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 cover with image and headline; 2 the problem; 3 the solution; 4 testimonial; 5 the ask (call to action); 6 details.

**Sort:** needs editing — Saterday → Saturday; you’re → your; “come along its free” → “Come along. It’s free!”; passive “volunteers are needed by us” → “We need volunteers”. Ready — trees and river; families, kids and dogs.

**Case study:** Kiernan was shocked by ocean rubbish on a solo round-the-world race; Clean Up Sydney Harbour on 8 January 1989 drew about 40,000 volunteers; the ask was simple, specific and time-bound; it became Clean Up Australia Day the next year, then Clean Up the World.

resources.label: Australian of the Year — Ian Kiernan AO

realityCheck: **Real groups make it real.** If a local group will use the best work, motivation goes up sharply.
**Check facts with the group.** Students shouldn’t invent statistics about a real organisation; use what the group publishes or tells them.
**Photos of real people need consent.** Use sketches or placeholders unless consent is given.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The edit sort is quick and students like finding errors.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank and a post template.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with four questions, features, and draft–feedback–revise.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: problem–solution–action, values, testimonials, and evaluating with evidence.
